extracted.intended_audience: researchers, grant program designers, research funders, and peer-review policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical study of how reviewer–proposal intellectual distance and proposal novelty affect grant review scores, with implications for reviewer matching and rubric design in research funding competitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to existing knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals fitting the current paradigm or existing knowledge tend to score better in peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers implicitly weight conformity, so rubrics that reward paradigm-aligned work will amplify this bias. Anti-pattern: favoring safe, incremental work at the expense of exploratory ideas. Scoring note: baseline reviewer behavior systematically prefers proposals that align with established knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiar methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals using techniques and methods the reviewer recognizes receive more favorable evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unfamiliar or novel methods may be penalized because reviewers default to evaluating what they know. Rubrics should explicitly account for methodological novelty or require reviewers to justify downgrades due to unfamiliarity to avoid undue bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictable outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals that present clear, predictable expected results (well-specified outcomes) are rated higher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers prefer projects with clear expected results; this can disadvantage exploratory or discovery-oriented proposals. Rubrics can mitigate by allowing separate evaluation dimensions for uncertainty and potential upside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance from reviewer's exact area (Intellectual distance / Goldilocks Zone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer–proposal intellectual distance matters: proposals exactly in a reviewer's expertise tend to receive lower scores, those moderately distant receive higher scores, and those very far receive lower scores because the reviewer cannot evaluate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study documents a 'Goldilocks' optimal distance—too close => over-critical/harsher standards/competition threat; too far => superficial evaluation. Effect size: substantial (≈1 point on a 10-point scale for close vs. distant). Implication for rubric design: matching algorithm should aim for moderate distance or deliberately mix distances across reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (Novelty penalty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly novel proposals receive systematically lower scores (a 'novelty penalty'); novelty was measured via unusual citation combinations and language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novelty penalty operates independently of intellectual distance and compounds with closeness (novel proposals close to an evaluator suffer the most). Rubrics that seek to reward novelty must explicitly counteract this baseline reviewer tendency (for example, via bonus points, separate novelty-dedicated criteria, or reviewer calibration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of close-expertise penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasons close-expertise reviewers give lower scores include harsher standards for their own area, perceiving proposals as competitive threats, and better detection of weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding mechanisms helps design interventions (blinding, calibrated scoring, reviewer guidance) to reduce undue penalization when reviewers are very close to the proposal topic. Scoring guidance: require explicit justification for low scores on close-expertise reviews to surface potential biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer–proposal matching algorithm tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: How evaluators are matched to proposals matters as much as rubric content: pure match-by-expertise minimizes Type I errors (funding bad proposals) but maximizes Type II errors (rejecting good novel proposals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers must balance false-positive vs false-negative risks when choosing matching rules. Consider mixed strategies rather than always maximizing expertise match if the program aims to fund novelty or high-risk, high-reward work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulation by reviewers at varying distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a set of reviewers with varied intellectual distances to a proposal (some close, some moderately distant, some far) produces more robust evaluations than concentrating reviewers who are all close experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize by assigning panels with intentionally diverse expertise distances or by combining specialist and generalist reviewers. Scoring note: triangulation can reduce both over-criticality from close experts and superficiality from distant reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for novelty-rewarding rubric features
rubrics_metrics.description: If a program's goal is to support novel or high-risk research, rubrics must include explicit features or mechanisms to reward novelty because baseline peer review penalizes it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: separate 'novelty' scoring dimension with calibration, explicit instructions to value high-risk/high-reward potential, reviewer incentives, or post-review interventions (e.g., programmatic re-weighting). Without such features, novelty-seeking programs will struggle under standard peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of structural limits on high-risk, high-reward funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard peer review structures and reviewer behaviors create systematic barriers that explain why programs aimed at high-risk, high-reward research have difficulty selecting and funding such proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program designers should not assume rubric content alone will overcome these structural effects; they must address matching, reviewer selection, calibration, and reward mechanisms collectively to change outcomes.
